title: Recognition of Indian art, Wild Magnolias and the library exhibit
summary: Cahn credits the Wild Magnolias' record, calls costumes museum pieces, and recalls a librarian who displayed them around 1967 and took heat.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: You think that will have some influence on it?

Bound to have some influence. I think everything has some influence. Oh, yeah. But I think the wild magnolia is, I think, Quint's record of Honda Wanda had some influence. Yeah, when Bo Dallas first did Honda Wanda. When he first did Honda Wanda. That was another movie. And I think the press releases, these people have been unrecognized. And they're great artists. The costumes themselves are a work of art. Yeah, I'll agree with that. And we have just negated the art that we have locally.

Which, these costumes are really museum pieces. In fact, they do have one in the Cabildo now. But we have gone through a, up until, I'd say, 1960, people just, let's say the power structure or whoever, just would not recognize the black art.
Well, they had recognized certain facets of black art, but this one they didn't.

But this one they wouldn't. And these, I remember the New Orleans librarian, his name was Cushman, displayed the costumes in the public library. And he caught, unshirted, hell for doing it. Really? This was in the middle 60s. I'd say around 67. Right. In that area. He had displayed. He thought that it should be displayed for the public to see. And I know some of the stuff he went through because he had guts enough to do that. Mm-hmm.
